title: Swollen Lymph Nodes After Drinking: Causes and When to Worry
excerpt: Why lymph nodes or glands can swell or ache after drinking, the common harmless causes, the rare pattern linked to Hodgkin lymphoma, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Swollen or painful lymph nodes after drinking? The common causes, the rare alcohol-pain sign linked to Hodgkin lymphoma, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most swollen or tender "glands" that people notice after a night of drinking have an ordinary explanation. You may be fighting off a cold or sore throat that happened to show up the same weekend, your salivary glands may be irritated from dehydration, or you may have strained your neck or irritated your throat by vomiting, smoking, or shouting over music. Those usually settle within a week or two. There is one pattern you should not ignore, though: **a lymph node that hurts within minutes of drinking alcohol, especially if it happens again and again.** That is a rare but well-documented warning sign of Hodgkin lymphoma, a type of blood cancer that is very treatable when it's found. It doesn't mean you have cancer. It does mean you should see a doctor and tell them exactly what you noticed.

**The quick rules:** If a lump in your neck, armpit, or groin hurts soon after you drink, book a doctor's appointment rather than waiting to see if it keeps happening. If a node is larger than about a fingertip, feels hard or rubbery, doesn't move when you press it, keeps growing, or is still there after two to four weeks, get it checked. If you also have fevers, drenching night sweats, unexplained weight loss, or itching all over, go sooner. If your glands are puffy for a few days alongside a sore throat or cold and then shrink, that's the normal immune response doing its job.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice, and it can't tell you what a lump in your body is. Only an examination, and sometimes tests, can do that. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if** you have trouble breathing or swallowing, swelling of your lips, tongue, or throat, hives with dizziness or faintness, drooling because you can't swallow, or a rapidly spreading hot, red, painful swelling in your neck with a high fever. **Book a doctor's visit soon if** a lymph node hurts or aches shortly after you drink alcohol (even once, and especially if it repeats); a node is bigger than about 1 cm (roughly the width of a fingertip), hard, fixed in place, or growing; a swollen node lasts more than two to four weeks; you have a lump just above your collarbone; or swelling comes with fever, night sweats that soak your sheets, weight loss you can't explain, constant tiredness, or itching all over. **Also tell a doctor plainly** if you get shaking, sweating, or a racing heart when you go a day without drinking. That can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous, and it's worth getting checked rather than toughing out.

## What Lymph Nodes Are and Why They Swell

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped filters spread throughout your body. You have hundreds of them, with clusters in your neck, under your jaw, behind your ears, in your armpits, and in your groin. They sit along a network of thin vessels that carry lymph, a clear fluid that collects from your tissues. As lymph passes through, the nodes trap germs, damaged cells, and debris, and they're packed with white blood cells that deal with whatever they catch.

When your body is fighting something, the nodes nearest the problem fill with extra immune cells and fluid. That's what makes them swell and feel tender. A sore throat makes the nodes under your jaw and along the sides of your neck puff up. A cut on your hand can make a node in your armpit swell. This is called reactive swelling, and it's the most common reason anyone has a swollen lymph node. It usually comes on over a day or two, is tender to the touch, and fades over one to three weeks as the infection clears.

A few features help doctors judge whether a node is the ordinary kind:

- **Size.** Normal nodes are usually smaller than about 1 cm across. Many people can feel small, soft nodes in their neck all the time, especially if they're slim.
- **Feel.** Reactive nodes tend to be soft or slightly firm, tender, and easy to move around under the skin. Nodes that feel hard, rubbery, or stuck in place get more attention.
- **Timing.** Swelling that appears with an obvious infection and shrinks over a couple of weeks is reassuring. Swelling that keeps growing or lasts more than a few weeks is not.
- **Location.** A node just above the collarbone is considered more concerning than one under the jaw, and doctors generally want to look at it promptly.
- **Company.** Swelling alongside fevers, drenching night sweats, or unexplained weight loss raises more questions than swelling on its own.

None of these features alone gives a diagnosis. They're the reasons a doctor might say "let's watch it for two weeks" in one case and "let's get a scan" in another.

## Can Alcohol Itself Make Lymph Nodes Swell?

For most people, no. Having a few drinks doesn't cause healthy lymph nodes to swell or hurt. What alcohol does is set up a handful of conditions that make swollen glands more likely, or that make you notice them more:

- **It can blunt your immune response for a while.** Research reviewed by the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) shows that a bout of heavy drinking temporarily weakens parts of the immune system, and that long-term heavy drinking makes people more prone to infections such as pneumonia. If you were already brewing a cold, a big night can make it hit harder, and your neck nodes react. Our guide to [alcohol and the immune system](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-immune-system-complete-health-impact-2025) covers this in more detail.
- **It dries you out.** Alcohol makes you pass more urine and reduces saliva. A dry mouth slows the flow through your salivary glands, which sit very close to the lymph nodes in your neck and are easy to mistake for them.
- **It irritates your throat.** Strong spirits, reflux, vomiting, snoring, smoke, and vaping all irritate the lining of your throat. Irritation and minor infections there can trigger reactive swelling in the nodes that drain the area.
- **Drinking often comes with other exposures.** Crowded bars, shared glasses, and late nights are a good way to catch a virus. The swollen glands show up a few days later, and it's natural to blame the drinks.

So if you notice puffy neck glands a day or two after drinking, along with a scratchy throat, a stuffy nose, or a general run-down feeling, the most likely story is a minor infection, not the alcohol itself.

## Lymph Nodes That Hurt Right After Drinking: The Pattern to Take Seriously

This is the part of the topic that sends many people searching, so here it is plainly.

Some people with **Hodgkin lymphoma**, a cancer of a type of white blood cell, notice that their swollen lymph nodes ache or hurt soon after they drink alcohol, sometimes within minutes and sometimes after just a small amount. The pain is usually felt in the affected nodes themselves, which may be in the neck, armpit, chest, or groin, and it can last from minutes to a few hours. Doctors have described this symptom in the medical literature for decades, and major cancer organizations such as the American Cancer Society and Cancer Research UK list it among the possible, uncommon symptoms of Hodgkin lymphoma.

Some important context so this lands the right way:

- **It's uncommon.** Only a small minority of people with Hodgkin lymphoma ever have alcohol-related pain. Most people with the disease never notice it, and most people who notice lymph node aches after drinking don't have lymphoma.
- **It's unusually specific when it does happen.** Pain triggered by alcohol isn't a typical feature of the common, harmless causes of swollen glands. That's why doctors treat it as a reason to examine you, rather than something to wait out.
- **Hodgkin lymphoma is one of the more treatable cancers.** Treatment has improved a great deal, and the outlook for most people, especially when it's found early, is good. Getting checked quickly is the thing that helps.
- **It has been reported with other conditions too.** Alcohol-triggered pain has occasionally been described in other lymphomas and some other conditions, which is another reason a proper examination matters more than self-diagnosis.

Nobody knows for certain why alcohol causes this pain. The leading ideas are that alcohol widens blood vessels and increases blood flow, which may raise pressure inside a node that's already swollen and enclosed in a tight capsule, and that alcohol may trigger the release of inflammatory chemical signals inside the affected tissue. A few older case reports noted that anti-inflammatory painkillers eased the pain, which has led some researchers to suspect inflammatory messengers called prostaglandins are involved. None of these explanations is settled.

### Other symptoms of Hodgkin lymphoma

If you've noticed alcohol-triggered node pain, it helps to know the other signs doctors will ask about. Having one or more of them alongside a swollen node makes an appointment more urgent:

- A painless swelling in the neck, armpit, or groin that doesn't go away
- Fevers that come and go without an obvious infection
- Night sweats heavy enough to soak your sheets or pajamas
- Losing weight without trying
- Itching of the skin, sometimes all over the body
- Persistent tiredness, a cough, or breathlessness

Doctors sometimes call the fever, night sweats, and weight loss "B symptoms." Mention any of them, even if they seem unrelated.

### What to say to your doctor

It's easy to forget the alcohol detail in the appointment, or to feel awkward bringing up your drinking. Don't skip it. It's a useful clinical clue, and doctors hear about drinking all the time. Try something like: "I have a lump in my neck, and it aches within about 20 minutes whenever I have a glass of wine. It's happened four or five times over the last month." Note where the lump is, roughly how big it feels, how long you've had it, whether it's changing, and any of the other symptoms above. A doctor will usually examine the area, ask about recent infections, and may order blood tests, an ultrasound or other scan, or refer you for a biopsy if the node looks suspicious.

## Neck Lymph Nodes Swollen After Drinking

The neck is where most people notice swelling, partly because it's easy to feel and partly because the throat, mouth, teeth, and sinuses all drain into nodes there. If your neck feels lumpy after drinking, the common culprits are:

- **A throat or upper airway infection.** Colds, flu, strep throat, and mononucleosis (mono, also called glandular fever) all make the nodes along the sides of the neck swell. Mono can make them quite large and is common in teens and young adults.
- **Throat irritation from the night out.** Vomiting, acid reflux, smoking, vaping, and shouting can leave your throat raw. If that's what you're dealing with, our guide to a [sore throat after drinking](/never-hungover/sore-throat-after-drinking) walks through each cause and what helps.
- **Dental problems.** An infected tooth or gum can make the nodes under your jaw swell and ache. Grinding your teeth or clenching your jaw while drinking can make the area sore too, which we cover in [jaw pain after drinking](/never-hungover/jaw-pain-after-drinking).
- **Muscle strain.** Sleeping in an awkward position after drinking can leave the muscles along the side of your neck sore and tight. A tender band of muscle can feel like a swollen gland, but it's usually longer and less defined than a node.

A reactive neck node tends to feel tender when you press it, gets better as the infection clears, and doesn't specifically hurt after a drink. A node that does hurt after drinking, or that keeps growing or lasts more than a few weeks, should be checked.

## Salivary Glands Swollen After Drinking (Often Mistaken for Lymph Nodes)

Many "swollen glands after drinking" turn out to be salivary glands rather than lymph nodes. You have three main pairs: the **parotid glands** in front of and just below your ears, the **submandibular glands** under the jaw on each side, and the **sublingual glands** under your tongue. They sit right next to lymph node clusters, so the two are easy to confuse.

Alcohol can affect the salivary glands in a few ways:

- **Dehydration and sluggish saliva flow.** When your mouth is dry, saliva moves slowly. That makes it easier for bacteria to travel up the gland's duct and cause an infection (sialadenitis), which shows up as a painful, swollen gland, sometimes with a bad taste or pus in the mouth. It's more common when you're dehydrated or unwell.
- **Salivary stones.** Small stones can form in the ducts, most often in the submandibular gland. The classic sign is swelling and pain under the jaw that gets worse when you eat, because the gland tries to release saliva past the blockage. Dehydration can make it worse.
- **Long-term heavy drinking.** Years of heavy drinking can cause a painless, soft swelling of both parotid glands, called sialadenosis. It gives the face a fuller look at the angle of the jaw and is often linked with liver disease and poor nutrition. It isn't a lymph node problem, but it is a sign worth raising with a doctor because of what it can point to.

If the swelling is in front of your ear or under your jaw, gets worse at mealtimes, or comes with a bad taste, a salivary gland is a likely source. Sipping water, sucking on sugar-free sour candies to get saliva flowing, gentle massage, and warm compresses are standard self-care for mild cases. A gland that's red, hot, very painful, or leaking pus, or that comes with a fever, needs a doctor, because it may need antibiotics.

## Lymph Node Pain in the Armpit or Groin After Drinking

Nodes in the armpit and groin are less likely to be affected by a throat infection, so swelling there has a different list of everyday causes: a small cut, insect bite, ingrown hair, or skin infection on the arm or leg; irritation from shaving or deodorant; a recent vaccine in that arm; or a strained muscle. These usually come with an obvious reason and fade in a week or two.

The rule about alcohol is the same wherever the node is. If a node in your armpit or groin hurts soon after you drink, or if a node in either place is firm, growing, or lasts more than a few weeks without a clear cause, see a doctor. Hodgkin lymphoma can affect nodes in these areas too, and breast changes in the armpit area should always be checked.

## Could It Be an Alcohol Allergy or Intolerance?

Sometimes people describe "swelling" after drinking when what they mean is a puffy, flushed face, a stuffy nose, or a swollen-feeling throat. Those symptoms are more likely to come from how your body handles alcohol and the other ingredients in drinks than from lymph nodes.

- **Alcohol intolerance** usually means your body is slow to clear acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product made when alcohol is broken down. The classic signs are flushing, a stuffy nose, a racing heart, and sometimes hives, often within minutes of a drink. It's common in people of East Asian descent who carry a less active version of the ALDH2 enzyme. Our guide to [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance) explains the signs and what helps.
- **Reactions to histamine, sulfites, or other ingredients** in wine, beer, and mixers can cause a stuffy nose, flushing, and hives in some people.
- **True allergy** to an ingredient in a drink (such as a grain, fruit, or additive) is rarer but can cause swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat and difficulty breathing. That's an emergency. See our guide to [alcohol allergy](/never-hungover/alcohol-allergy) for how to tell the difference.

These reactions don't typically cause a distinct, painful lump in a lymph node. If what you feel is a specific lump that aches after drinking, treat it as a lymph node issue and get it examined.

## Mono, Other Infections, and Drinking

Mono deserves its own mention because it's common in the age group that drinks most socially and it causes large, tender neck nodes along with fatigue, fever, and a very sore throat. Mono often inflames the liver and can enlarge the spleen. Doctors generally advise avoiding alcohol while you recover, because your liver is already under strain, and avoiding contact sports for several weeks because of the risk to an enlarged spleen. If you've been diagnosed with mono or any infection and are taking medication, ask your doctor or pharmacist when it's safe to drink again.

The same advice applies more broadly. If your glands are up because you're fighting something off, skipping alcohol for a few days gives your immune system and your sleep a better chance to do their job.

## What You Can Do at Home (and What Not to Do)

For ordinary reactive swelling with a cold or sore throat, the basics help:

- **Rest and fluids.** Drink water steadily, sleep, and give your immune system time.
- **Warm compresses.** A warm, damp cloth on a tender neck node or salivary gland can ease the ache.
- **Over-the-counter pain relief, used carefully.** If you need something for pain, follow the label and be cautious about mixing painkillers with alcohol. Acetaminophen and heavy drinking can strain the liver, and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen can irritate the stomach. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the risks.
- **Skip the drinks while you're unwell.** Alcohol worsens sleep and can make a sore throat or dehydration worse.
- **Keep a short note.** Write down when you first noticed the lump, where it is, roughly how big it is, and whether drinking seems to make it ache. That record makes a doctor's visit much more useful.

What not to do:

- **Don't keep testing it.** If a node hurts after a drink, you don't need to drink again to "make sure." Once is enough reason to book an appointment.
- **Don't treat alcohol-triggered pain with painkillers and move on.** Even if a painkiller helps, it doesn't tell you why the node hurts.
- **Don't squeeze, poke, or massage a node hard.** Pressing it constantly can keep it sore and makes it harder to judge whether it's shrinking.
- **Don't wait months.** A node that hasn't gone away in two to four weeks should be looked at, whether or not alcohol is involved.

## A Simple Way to Think About It

Most swollen glands after a night out fall into the "explained and improving" group: there's an obvious cold, sore throat, tooth problem, or night of vomiting, the swelling is tender, and it fades within a week or two. That group is very common and rarely serious.

A small number fall into the "check this" group: a node that hurts after drinking alcohol, a node that's hard, fixed, or growing, a node above the collarbone, swelling that lasts more than two to four weeks, or swelling with fevers, night sweats, weight loss, or itching. That group isn't a diagnosis. It's simply the set of signs that means a doctor should take a look, and an early look is what you want.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

It's worth being clear: no supplement treats swollen lymph nodes, and there is no good evidence that DHM (dihydromyricetin) or any other hangover product prevents them or the alcohol-triggered pain described above, so we don't recommend any product for this symptom. If a node hurts after drinking, the right step is a doctor's visit. For ordinary next-day symptoms that clearly aren't about a lump, our guides to [hangover symptoms](/never-hungover/hangover-symptoms) and [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) cover what actually helps. For anything involving lumps, persistent swelling, or pain triggered by alcohol, get examined first.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do my lymph nodes swell after drinking alcohol?**

Usually because something else is going on at the same time. A cold, sore throat, mono, dental infection, or throat irritation from vomiting, smoking, or reflux makes nearby nodes swell as your immune system responds, and a night of drinking can coincide with or worsen these. Dehydration can also inflame the salivary glands, which are easy to mistake for lymph nodes. If a node specifically hurts soon after you drink, see a doctor, because that is a rare warning sign of Hodgkin lymphoma.

**Is pain in lymph nodes after drinking alcohol always a sign of cancer?**

No. Most people who notice achy glands after drinking don't have cancer, and most people with Hodgkin lymphoma never have alcohol-related pain. But pain in a lymph node that starts soon after drinking is a recognized, if uncommon, symptom of Hodgkin lymphoma and isn't typical of the common harmless causes. That's why it's worth a doctor's visit rather than waiting to see if it happens again.

**How long does it take for alcohol-related lymph node pain to start?**

People with Hodgkin lymphoma who get this symptom typically describe pain in the affected nodes within minutes of drinking, sometimes after only a small amount, and it can last from minutes to a few hours. Swollen glands that appear a day or two after a night out, along with cold or throat symptoms, are much more likely to be an infection.

**Can dehydration from alcohol cause swollen glands?**

It can contribute. Dehydration reduces saliva flow, which makes salivary gland infections and blockages from salivary stones more likely. That causes swelling and pain under the jaw or in front of the ear, often worse when eating. Dehydration on its own doesn't usually make lymph nodes swell. Drink water, and see a doctor if a gland becomes red, hot, very painful, or comes with fever.

**When should I worry about a swollen lymph node?**

See a doctor if a node hurts after drinking alcohol, is larger than about 1 cm, feels hard or rubbery, doesn't move, keeps growing, sits just above your collarbone, or lasts more than two to four weeks. Go sooner if it comes with fevers, drenching night sweats, unexplained weight loss, or itching all over. Get emergency care for trouble breathing or swallowing or a rapidly spreading hot, red neck swelling with high fever.

**Can heavy drinking cause swelling in the face or near the ears?**

Yes. Long-term heavy drinking can cause a soft, painless swelling of the parotid salivary glands in front of the ears, called sialadenosis, which gives the face a fuller look at the jaw. It isn't a lymph node problem, but it's often linked to liver disease and poor nutrition, so it's worth raising with a doctor.

**Should I stop drinking if I have swollen lymph nodes?**

It's sensible to skip alcohol while you're fighting an infection, because it can disrupt sleep and immune function. If drinking makes a node hurt, stop drinking and see a doctor rather than continuing to test it. If you've been diagnosed with mono, doctors generally advise avoiding alcohol while your liver recovers.

**Can DHM prevent swollen lymph nodes after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents swollen lymph nodes or alcohol-triggered lymph node pain, and it shouldn't be used to manage either. DHM is studied for alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms, mostly in animal research with limited human data. A lump that hurts after drinking needs a doctor's examination, not a supplement.
